clue.text: Chances of US mum fighting to keep husband largely the same

indicators.note: the jumbled letters hold the next piece inside them, as a keeper holds something
the words chances of US mum are in a scrap with each other, so their letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: these words are taken letter for letter as the raw material

explanation.surface: An American mother's prospects stay about the same as long as she holds on to her husband.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes things so alike that there is little to choose between them, which is near enough being identical.

clue.text: Decorating trouble — call to engage handyman in the end

parts.note: ado is fuss or bother

indicators.note: the call takes on the next letter inside it, as an employer engages a worker

parts.note: to ring is to phone

indicators.note: only the final letter of handyman is used

parts.note: the last letter of handyman

explanation.surface: Someone redecorating has a problem and phones to hire a handyman.
explanation.definitionFit: To adorn is to ornament something, so adorning is the act of embellishing a room or object.

clue.text: Be behind redhead in shadow

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the word for shadow

parts.note: to tail someone is to follow and watch them, as a detective shadows a suspect
the head, or first letter, of red

explanation.surface: A detective is told to stay at the back while following a red-haired suspect.
explanation.definitionFit: To trail in a race or contest is to lag behind the others.

clue.text: Exploits at work finally impress weaklings

parts.note: to milk a situation is to exploit it for all it is worth
op is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: only the last letter of impress is taken

parts.note: the final letter of impress

explanation.surface: Someone's feats on the job at last win over the doubters who thought them feeble.
explanation.definitionFit: A milksop is a timid, ineffectual person, so the plural names a group of feeble, spineless types.

clue.text: Rents show no restraint

wordplay.note: read as two kinds of rent: to let is to rent out, and a rip is a rent or tear

explanation.surface: A complaint that landlords' charges are spiralling out of control.
explanation.walkthrough: The single word supplies both halves, since let and rip are each a sense of rent.
explanation.definitionFit: To let rip is an idiom for acting or speaking without holding back.

clue.text: Same agent changed what player's called

indicators.note: the letters of same agent are altered into another order

parts.note: the words taken letter for letter as the raw material

explanation.surface: An actor keeps the same representative but alters how they are billed.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer's professional pseudonym is the name an actor, or player, is known by on stage.

clue.text: Lack of variety cycling — correct? Let me think!

indicators.note: the word for correct goes round, its last letter moving to the front

parts.note: to edit a text is to correct it
um is the hesitation sound someone makes while thinking

explanation.surface: Someone hesitates over whether going round and round on a bike is a monotonous pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: Tedium is boring monotony, the dullness that comes from sameness and repetition.

clue.text: The wife and a 'friend' messed around inside, so it's not 17 down

indicators.note: the letter for around is placed within the jumbled letters
the letters of the wife, a and friend are messed up into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written; the quotation marks hint at a false friend
c, for circa, means around a date

explanation.surface: A wife and a so-called friend have been fooling around behind someone's back, which is hardly business as usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 17 down is THE USUAL, so the definition asks for something out of the ordinary.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done with a difference has an unusual twist, the opposite of the ordinary routine.

clue.text: Stress over work? Quite the opposite

indicators.note: tells the solver to turn over into its opposite before putting the pieces together

parts.note: over is swapped for its opposite, under
a line is a line of work, an occupation

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they are suffering from strain caused by overwork, and is told the reverse is true.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap over for its opposite and the phrase reads under work, put together as under plus a line of work.
explanation.definitionFit: To underline a point is to emphasise it, as drawing a line beneath words gives them emphasis.

clue.text: Amuse daughter going round water feature in capital

indicators.note: what remains is turned round to read the other way
the daughter leaves, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: to divert someone is to entertain them

explanation.surface: A parent keeps a daughter entertained as they walk round a fountain in a city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Trevi is the famous Baroque fountain in Rome, Italy's capital, where tourists throw coins.

clue.text: Make a mistake feeding rustic poet

indicators.note: the word for a mistake goes into the rustic's mouth, as food would

parts.note: a hick is an unsophisticated country person
to err is to make a mistake

explanation.surface: A countryside poet slips up while feeding something.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Herrick was a 17th-century English lyric writer, author of 'Gather ye rosebuds while ye may'.

clue.text: One hour's spent describing Meg's backside — cheeky!

indicators.note: describing is read as drawing a line around, so the scrambled letters go round the next piece
spent means used up and worn out, so these letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: one is I, set beside the word hours as written

indicators.note: the backside of a word is its last letter, here taken from Meg's

explanation.surface: Someone wastes an hour sketching Meg's bottom, a rather saucy pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spent' scrambles I plus HOURS into ROUISH, and 'describing' wraps that round G, the last letter of Meg's, chosen by 'backside'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe playful impudence, so they are synonyms as adjectives for a mischievous manner.

clue.text: Meet round side and do a runner

indicators.note: the word for meet goes round the letter

parts.note: fit and meet both mean suitable or proper
L for left, one side

explanation.surface: Someone joins a gathering, goes round one side and then makes off.
explanation.definitionFit: To flit is to move house or leave secretly to avoid debts, which is what doing a runner means in British slang.

clue.text: Not still angry?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: hopping, jumping about rather than keeping still

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone has calmed down yet.
explanation.walkthrough: Still reads as 'yet', but here it means motionless; the phrase literally pictures someone jumping about, and idiomatically means furious.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means extremely cross, while its first word literally describes someone leaping up and down.

clue.text: Desk twice ransacked — this could not be worse

indicators.note: the desk and the word twice are turned over, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the words taken letter for letter as the raw material

explanation.surface: Finding one's desk turned over a second time is the worst possible outcome.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of wicked describes the most evil thing, one beyond which nothing is worse.

clue.text: Pets whose traditional enemies doubled at first

indicators.note: the first letter, D, is 500 in Roman numerals; doubled it becomes 1000, or M

parts.note: doggies, the dogs that cats are traditionally at war with

explanation.surface: Pet owners whose old foes have increased twofold from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: Roman numerals do the work: D is 500, and twice that is M, 1000.
explanation.definitionFit: Moggies is British slang for cats, especially ordinary domestic ones kept as household animals.

clue.text: Break with former court favourite? Boycott's no good!

parts.note: Tim Henman, the British tennis player long adored by Wimbledon crowds

indicators.note: the cricketer's name is said to have no good in it, so the letter for good is removed

parts.note: Geoffrey Boycott, the Yorkshire and England cricketer, known as Geoff

explanation.surface: A tennis darling takes a rest, while a famous cricketer is judged useless.
explanation.walkthrough: Tim Henman was a much-loved British tennis player; Geoffrey Boycott is a former England opening batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: Time off is a period of rest from work, a holiday or interval.

clue.text: America detaining university lecturer — that's reportedly in order

definitions.note: the drink a pub regular orders, according to the barman, is 'the usual'

indicators.note: the country holds the next letter inside it

parts.note: the USA, written with its article

explanation.surface: America holds a university academic, which apparently is all quite proper.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on in order: what is said to be ordered by a regular customer.
explanation.definitionFit: A regular customer asks for their customary drink or meal simply by saying this phrase.

clue.text: Inflexible — read nothing but rubbish

indicators.note: the letters are treated as rubbish and scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
O looks like zero, nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A stubborn reader will consume nothing but trash.
explanation.definitionFit: An obdurate person is stubbornly unwilling to change their mind, unbending.

clue.text: Here, time's up!

definitions.meaning: points to a place rather than a moment
reads as a referee's call, but means the time is displayed up high

explanation.surface: An announcement that the allotted time has run out.
explanation.walkthrough: Time's up sounds like a deadline, but literally the time is shown aloft on a tall building.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall structure bearing a clock face high above the street shows the hour to everyone.

clue.text: Heavy metal backing musician covering Iron Maiden's originals

indicators.note: the whole is read backwards
the musician goes over those letters, enclosing them

parts.note: muso is informal for a musician

indicators.note: the first letters of Iron and Maiden

parts.note: the band name, whose two words supply their opening letters

explanation.surface: A musician playing backing for a heavy metal band covers the first songs of Iron Maiden.
explanation.definitionFit: Osmium is a very dense metallic element, among the heaviest naturally occurring substances.

clue.text: Will being violent once here wound? Very upset on the surface

indicators.note: the reversed word forms the outside, with the wound inside it
turned over, read backwards in a down clue

parts.note: so, as in 'so good'
a scar is the mark of a wound

explanation.surface: Was it here that Will lashed out and left an injury, the surface sorely upset?
explanation.walkthrough: Will Smith slapped Chris Rock on stage at the 2022 Oscars ceremony.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Awards, where Will Smith struck Chris Rock in 2022, are informally named after their statuettes.

clue.text: Fish round lake doing nothing

indicators.note: the fish surrounds the letter for lake

parts.note: the ide is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A fish circles a lake, idling.
explanation.definitionFit: Being idle is being inactive, not working or occupied.

clue.text: Sailor isn't entertaining creature of the night

indicators.note: the words sailor isn't hold the answer within them, as a host holds a guest

parts.note: the run of letters across sailor isn't holds the creature

explanation.surface: A sailor declines to host a nocturnal animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The loris is a slow-moving nocturnal primate of South and South-East Asia.

clue.text: Hill on track heading west — I start to climb moving on

indicators.note: travelling right to left, so the name reads backwards

parts.note: Damon Hill, the 1996 Formula One world champion, a Hill on the racetrack
taken as written

indicators.note: only the first letter of climb is taken

parts.note: the first letter of climb

explanation.surface: A walker on a hill path heads west and begins to climb.
explanation.walkthrough: Hill is not a hill at all but racing driver Damon Hill.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomadic people keep travelling from place to place rather than settling.

clue.text: Cause of suffering — not having a second bottle!

indicators.note: the word for bottle must go without the letter a, so it is dropped

parts.note: bottle is British slang for nerve or courage
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something painful, a drinker says, is being refused another bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottle is British slang for courage, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: A scourge is a whip, and figuratively anything that causes great affliction or misery.

clue.text: Son and his mates playing in drives

definitions.meaning: Heung-min Son and his teammates at Tottenham Hotspur
to spur is to urge on

explanation.surface: A boy and his friends play out in the driveways.
explanation.walkthrough: Son is the South Korean striker who played for Tottenham Hotspur, the London club known as Spurs.
explanation.definitionFit: The club's nickname fits the team, and spurs as a verb means urges forward, as a rider goads a horse.

clue.text: Foreign article is clear-sighted

indicators.note: the words article is are made strange, rearranged into an unfamiliar order

parts.note: the words taken letter for letter as the raw material

explanation.surface: A piece in a foreign paper is said to be perceptive.
explanation.definitionFit: A realistic person sees things as they are, a sensible and practical outlook.
